Endurance training elicits a broad but non-uniform, coordinated molecular response across rat organs, organized into a few reproducible tissue axes.

EXTENT OF COORDINATION
- Of 279,002 sex x timepoint contrasts on 35,441 training-regulated features (all training FDR < 0.05), 100,775 (36.1%) are timewise significant (|z| >= 2); the result is threshold-insensitive (alternative definitions flag 35.2-36.9%, r >= 0.94 with the primary).
- Response breadth is highest in the contractile tissues: heart (46.0% of its contrasts timewise significant) and gastrocnemius (46.2%), vs colon 20.3% and spleen 25.5%. Effect magnitude shows the inverse pattern: BAT's significant contrasts are largest (median |log2FC| 0.99; mean 1.27), heart's smallest among major tissues (median 0.24).
- Coordination across molecular layers: RNA and protein effect sizes correlate strongly in glycolytic muscle (SKM-GN r = 0.81, n = 80 shared genes) and moderately in lung (r = 0.61), but weakly in heart (r = 0.13), WAT (r = 0.11) and liver (r = 0.29). Union across the 9 omic layers multiplies the detectable response 4-7x over proteome alone (e.g. LIVER 5,926 entities vs 1,039 proteome features); only ~50-100 genes per tissue are regulated at both RNA and protein level.
- Coordination across sexes is pathway-level, not feature-level: only 12.8% of features are timewise significant in both sexes at the same timepoint; overlap of significant sets is at or below chance in all 54 adequately powered tissue x assay cells (median 0.98x independence expectation; colon transcriptome Jaccard 0.20), yet oxidative-metabolism enrichments fire in both sexes.
- Oxidative-metabolism programs anchor the shared response: FAO genes enriched in BAT (OR = 17.6, q < 1e-4) and heart (OR = 11.0, q < 1e-4); OXPHOS/mito genes in BAT (OR = 11.5), skeletal muscle (SKM-VL OR = 12.6, SKM-GN OR = 6.1), colon (OR = 4.7) and kidney (OR = 3.5), all q <= 1e-3. The response keeps growing with training: feature counts peak at 8 weeks in 9 of 17 tissues (liver 4,434; adrenal 3,406; heart 2,397; BAT 2,394), while WAT, lung, small intestine and hippocampus peak at 1 week.

MOST SIMILAR TISSUES (Pearson r of mean log2FC over shared regulated entities, n >= 30 shared entities required; top pairs stable across timepoints and across significance-restricted vs unselected means, rank rho = 0.83)
1. KIDNEY - gastrocnemius (SKM-GN): r = +0.71, n = 188, 70% same direction - the top pair overall, present at every timepoint; both co-upregulate oxidative phosphorylation.
2. BLOOD - SPLEEN: r = +0.62, n = 325, 81% same direction - the immune axis; the two cluster alone at every wave except 4 weeks.
3. ADRENAL - subcutaneous WAT: r = +0.57, best-supported pair (n = 728); with LIVER and PLASMA they form an endocrine-adipose-hepatic cluster (hierarchical clustering, k = 8: {blood, spleen}, {adrenal, liver, plasma, WAT}, {cortex, heart}, {hippocampus, kidney, lung, gastrocnemius, VL muscle}, and singleton BAT, colon, hypothalamus).
4. CORTEX - HEART (+0.65) and HIPPOCAMPUS - SKM-GN (+0.64): brain and muscle share direction of response.
5. The two skeletal muscles are the most directionally concordant of all pairs (SKM-GN - SKM-VL, 93% same sign, r = +0.53); heart vs VL muscle is the most anti-correlated pair (r = -0.54) - cardiac and skeletal muscle adapt differently.

Globally 59% of scoreable tissue pairs are positive (median r = 0.27): coordination is real and pathway-anchored (oxidative metabolism, shared between kidney, muscle, BAT and heart; immune programs shared between blood and spleen; endocrine programs shared by adrenal, WAT, liver and plasma) but not uniform - BAT, colon and hypothalamus each respond idiosyncratically, and BAT inverts its FAO/energy-buffer signature between 1 week (+0.34 log2FC; phosphocreatine +3.28) and 8 weeks (-0.82; phosphocreatine +1.80).

Main caveats: the file is pre-filtered at FDR < 0.05 and assay coverage differs per tissue (liver 9 layers vs blood 1), so per-tissue response sizes are not comparable in absolute terms; pairwise correlations rest on shared-entity sets (median n = 83) and are mildly inflated by conditioning on significance (bounded by an unselected-mean replication); ovary, testes and vena cava lack timewise statistics and are excluded from time-resolved conclusions.

Quantitative evidence, code and figures: trace.md, analysis/README.md, analysis/output/ (tables and 300-dpi figures).

Question: Which proteins correlate with changes in body composition (fat percentage and breast volume) following feminizing GAHT?

Data: 5,278 plasma proteins (Olink Explore-HT) tested for mixed-linear-model association (random intercept per participant; adjusted for age and baseline BMI) with percent body fat and with breast volume. Significance threshold: Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
- Percent body fat: 38 significant proteins (2 positive, 36 negative); 11 at adj p < 0.01.
- Breast volume: 249 significant proteins (12 positive, 237 negative); 78 at adj p < 0.01.
- Overlap between traits: 28 proteins significant for both (Fisher exact OR = 63.6, p = 5.1e-30); effect directions are concordant in 28/28. Genome-wide Spearman correlation of the two association profiles: rho = +0.28 (p = 1.8e-93).
- Total distinct proteins significantly associated with at least one trait: 259 of 5,278 (4.9%).

PERCENT BODY FAT — PROTEINS AND ASSOCIATIONS
Positive (higher protein with higher fat %):
- LEP (leptin): beta = +0.196, adj p = 5.5e-4 — the single strongest fat hit; canonical adipocyte-derived adiposity marker.
- CFC1: beta = +0.071, adj p = 0.025 — EGF-CFC developmental signaling co-receptor.
Negative (higher protein with lower fat %; strongest 15 by effect size):
- MAPK4: -0.217 (adj p 0.047)
- DEFB4A (beta-defensin 4A): -0.209 (0.014)
- MUC1 (epithelial mucin): -0.167 (0.015)
- CA6 (carbonic anhydrase VI, glandular secretion): -0.139 (5.5e-4; tied smallest p with LEP and PLB1)
- MMP3 (matrix metalloproteinase-3): -0.112 (0.015)
- CCL24 (eotaxin-2): -0.102 (0.0018)
- PSG1 (pregnancy-specific beta-1-glycoprotein): -0.098 (0.0029)
- PI3 / elafin (epithelial antiprotease): -0.096 (0.013)
- PPY (pancreatic polypeptide, satiety hormone): -0.094 (0.031)
- PGLYRP3 (peptidoglycan recognition protein 3): -0.085 (0.0029)
- PLB1 (phospholipase B1): -0.084 (5.5e-4)
- CYTL1: -0.076 (0.0029)
- IVL (involucrin): -0.074 (0.010)
- CST6 (cystatin E/M): -0.070 (0.0049)
- CLSTN2: -0.064 (0.021)
Further significant negatives: VIT, FGFBP2, ENDOU, SPINK5, CBLIF, SOST (sclerostin, Wnt antagonist), ENPP5, LY75, KLK13, IGSF21, DSG3, WIF1 (Wnt-inhibitory factor 1), ART3, RELT, XPNPEP2, DPEP1, KLK6, CEACAM19, ITGAV, COL15A1, CRTAC1.
Interpretation: the fat signature is dominated by inverse correlations with innate-immunity/granulocyte proteins (CCL24, PGLYRP3, DEFB4A, PI3, FGFBP2, CA6, KLK6), epithelial/glandular-secretory proteins (MUC1, IVL, DSG3, SPINK5, CST6) and ECM-remodeling/Wnt-antagonist proteins (MMP3, COL15A1, ITGAV, WIF1, SOST). LEP is the expected positive adiposity marker; the Wnt-antagonist decreases (WIF1, SOST) are permissive for adipogenesis in the Wnt-adipogenesis literature.

BREAST VOLUME — PROTEINS AND ASSOCIATIONS
Positive (higher protein with larger breast volume) — a coherent mammary-gland-activation signature:
- CXCL13: +0.00592, adj p 6.7e-4 — largest positive effect of all 249 hits.
- LEP (leptin): +0.00527, adj p 3.1e-3 — the only protein positively associated with BOTH traits.
- PRL (prolactin): +0.00435, adj p 2.8e-4 — master mammogenic hormone.
- PAEP (milk protein beta-lactoglobulin / glycodelin): +0.00249, adj p 0.030 — direct secretory-epithelium readout.
- CCL28 (+0.00215, 0.033), TNFAIP6 (+0.00160, 0.027), VEGFD (lymphangiogenic; +0.00107, 0.038), CD70 (+0.00107, 0.046), MZB1 (+0.00101, 0.045), EDA2R (+0.00088, 0.044), GAPDH (+0.00080, 0.0077), RAB27B (secretory GTPase; +0.00066, 0.049).
Negative (higher protein with smaller breast volume; strongest by effect size / significance):
- INSL3 (insulin-like 3, Leydig-cell androgen-responsive hormone): -0.01515, adj p = 3.3e-5 — the single most significant association in the entire table; direct endocrine readout of androgen/testicular suppression on GAHT.
- SPINT3: -0.02035, adj p 3.1e-4 (largest magnitude).
- Also: EDDM3B (epididymal protease inhibitor; -0.0069, 5.9e-4), TEX101 (testis-expressed; -0.0045, 0.025), DEFB4A (-0.0058), MUC1 (-0.0053), PROK1 (-0.0043), PM20D1 (-0.0043), MMP3 (-0.0035), CCK (-0.0036), NPY (-0.0039), TOP1, CUL7, MME, PTPRH, and ~220 more.
Interpretation: positive hits (PRL, PAEP, CXCL13, CCL28, MZB1, RAB27B, TNFAIP6, VEGFD) mark growing ductal-lobular tissue with secretory/lactational differentiation and accompanying mucosal lymphoid and lymphatic expansion. The dominant negative hits are male-reproductive-axis proteins (INSL3, TEX101, EDDM3B, SPINT3) collapsing under antiandrogen + estrogen therapy, plus broad ECM/metabolic declines.

PROTEINS SIGNIFICANT FOR BOTH TRAITS (28, all concordant in sign; 27 negative, LEP positive)
LEP (+/+), and concordant-negative: KLK6, CEACAM19, DPEP1, XPNPEP2, IGSF21, LY75, ENPP5, SOST, CBLIF, SPINK5, ENDOU, FGFBP2, VIT, CLSTN2, CST6, IVL, CYTL1, PLB1, PGLYRP3, PPY, PI3, PSG1, CCL24, MMP3, CA6, MUC1, DEFB4A.
LEP is the standout shared marker: secreted in proportion to fat mass and a known permissive factor in mammary ductal outgrowth, hence positively linked to both fat accretion and breast enlargement.

BIOLOGICAL SUMMARY
Feminizing GAHT body-composition change is accompanied by: (1) a leptin-scale increase tracking adipose accretion (LEP is the top and only strong positive fat hit); (2) emergence of a mammary secretory/glandular proteomic signature specific to breast volume (PRL, PAEP, CXCL13, CCL28, RAB27B, TNFAIP6, VEGFD); (3) suppression of androgen/testicular-axis proteins (INSL3 — most significant hit in the table — TEX101, EDDM3B, SPINT3); and (4) a broadly inverse systemic inflammatory/granulocyte and epithelial-secretory profile shared by both traits (CCL24, PGLYRP3, DEFB4A, PI3, MMP3, MUC1, CA6, CST6, CYTL1, PSG1...).

LIMITATIONS
- Correlational cross-sectional-style mixed-model coefficients (random intercept per participant, adjusted only for age and baseline BMI); no causal or temporal direction can be inferred from these numbers alone.
- Only adjusted p-values are provided (no raw p-values, confidence intervals, sample sizes, or per-arm CPA-vs-SPIRO coefficients); the authors' FDR cannot be recomputed or stratified.
- Breast-volume units are not stated in the file; effect magnitudes are not comparable across the two traits (only signs and within-trait ranks).
- At FDR 0.05 across 5,278 tests, roughly 2 of the 38 fat hits and 12 of the 249 breast-volume hits are expected false positives; hits near adj p ~ 0.05 should be treated cautiously, whereas LEP, INSL3, PRL, CXCL13, PAEP, CA6, CCL24, PGLYRP3 (adj p <= 1e-3) are individually robust.

Key references: Considine et al. 1996 (NEJM 334:292; PMID 8532024; leptin-fat proportionality); Ben-Jonathan et al. 2008 (Endocr Rev 29:1; PMID 18048726; prolactin mammogenic role); Hennighausen & Robinson 2005 (Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 6:715; PMID 16136448; mammary gland networks); Ivell & Anand-Ivell 2018 (Hum Reprod Update 24:537; PMID 29246935; INSL3 as Leydig-cell androgen-responsive marker); Ross et al. 2000 (Science 289:950; PMID 10976015; Wnt suppression of adipogenesis); Benjamini & Hochberg 1995 (J R Stat Soc B 57:289; FDR methodology); UniProt (uniprot.org; protein function annotations).

Answer: Which expanded Tex-relevant TCR clonotypes are shared across multiple patients (public) and could serve as TCR-T candidates?

METHOD (from GSE243013_T_with_TCR_annotation.csv.gz, 434,458 T cells / 231 NSCLC patients, joined to mmc1.csv clinical data):
- Tex-relevant = clonotype has cells in CD8T_Tex_HAVCR2 (progenitor-exhausted) and/or CD8T_terminal_Tex_LAYN (terminally exhausted) compartments.
- Expanded = clonotype flagged "expanded" in the data (equivalent to >=3 cells; verified: min cells of expanded = 3, max of non-expanded = 2).
- Shared across patients: clonotype IDs are patient-private (0/255,451 IDs occur in >1 patient), so sharing was assessed on the receptor-defining amino-acid TRB CDR3 sequence; candidates with an identical TRB+TRA CDR3 pair across patients are flagged as the strongest evidence (fully public alpha-beta receptors).

FILTER FUNNEL: 434,458 cells -> 41,337 Tex cells (31,093 HAVCR2+ + 10,244 LAYN+) -> 5,581 expanded Tex-relevant clonotypes (5,298 unique TRB CDR3 sequences) -> 35 sequences shared by >=2 patients (39 patients total; 14 of them with co-shared TRB+TRA CDR3 pairs).

TOP-RANKED CANDIDATES:

Tier 1 - broadest sharing (>=3 patients):
1. CASSLGYEQYF (TRBJ2-7; TRBV11-2/TRBV19/TRBV27/TRBV28/TRBV5-4 by patient) - 5 patients (P268, P289, P453, P470, P471), 33 cells, 58% in Tex (15 CD8T_Tex_HAVCR2, 4 CD8T_terminal_Tex_LAYN), expanded in all 5 patients; patient responses: 2x pCR, 1x MPR.

Answer: Yes — 6 months of feminizing GAHT significantly remodels the plasma proteome (dominated by broad decreases), and the changes differ between the CPA and SPIRO antiandrogen regimens in both magnitude of shared effects and in arm-specific proteins.

Analysis summary (paired design, 40 subjects x baseline/6 months; 20 per arm; 4,897 detectable Olink Explore HT assays out of 5,420; BH FDR):

1) Proteins significantly altered after 6 months (within-regimen paired t-tests on DeltaNPX):
- CPA arm: 268/4,897 assays at BH q<0.05 — 256 decreased, 12 increased.
  Largest decreases: SPINT3 -7.91 NPX, INSL3 -5.34, EDDM3B -2.67, TEX101 -2.08, RBP1 -2.04, ACRV1 -1.37.
  Increases: CXCL13 +1.84 (q=1e-4), LEP +1.50 (q=1e-4), PRL +1.38 (q~1e-5).
- SPIRO arm: 129/4,897 at BH q<0.05 — 126 decreased, 3 increased.
  Largest decreases: SPINT3 -3.52 (q=0.006), ATP5F1D -2.86 (q=0.043), INSL3 -1.75 (q=0.016), EDDM3B -1.32 (q=0.006), TEX101 -0.91 (q=0.034).
  Significant increase: LEP +1.04 (q=0.028).
- Both arms shift globally downward (70.8% / 77.8% of assays negative; Wilcoxon signed-rank p~1e-221 and <1e-300).

2) Regimen x time interaction (does the change differ between CPA and SPIRO?):
Two-stage Welch contrast (delta_SPIRO - delta_CPA, BH-corrected) finds 10 proteins at q<0.05; a full per-assay mixed model NPX ~ time*regimen + (1|subject) confirms them and adds 17 more at q<0.05 (the two interaction p-value vectors agree at Spearman rho = 0.9999). Headline interaction hits (Delta CPA vs Delta SPIRO; positive delta_diff = CPA falls more):
- INSL3: -5.34 vs -1.75 (diff +3.60, q=2e-5) — Leydig-cell hormone under LH control; CPA suppresses the HPG axis far more strongly.
- SPINT3: -7.91 vs -3.52 (diff +4.39, q=0.004).
- PRL: +1.38 vs +0.19 (diff -1.19, q=4e-5) — prolactin rises only under CPA, consistent with its dopamine-D2 antagonism.
- CXCL13: +1.84 vs +0.21 (diff -1.63, q=0.004) — CPA-specific B-cell chemokine signal.
- NELL1, CFC1, SPOCK1, EDDM3B, RTBDN, REN complete the q<0.05 set; REN falls under CPA (-0.56) but rises under SPIRO (+0.19), matching spironolactone's known hyperreninemic mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade.
Overlap between arms: 52 proteins significant in both arms at q<0.05, 52/52 in the same direction (51 down), a ~10-fold enrichment over chance (5.4 expected), but the global per-protein response vectors correlate at only Spearman rho = 0.044 — a shared androgen-dependent core (INSL3, SPINT3, TEX101, EDDM3B, ACRV1, MSMB, PROK1, MUC1, CA6 all down in both; LEP up in both) plus large regimen-specific components.

Biological interpretation: CPA suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, collapsing LH-dependent secretion (INSL3 3x lower than SPIRO, deeper falls in epididymal/seminal proteins) and, uniquely, increases prolactin; spironolactone's peripheral androgen-receptor blockade produces qualitatively similar but milder shared changes plus a distinct renin response. Concordant rises in leptin and SHBG-like liver markers reflect estrogen-driven adiposity and hepatic effects common to both regimens.

Key limitations: 20 pairs per arm (interaction tests modestly powered); no covariate data (age, BMI, estrogen dose, gonadotropins); single plate (no batch adjustment possible); LOD reconstructed from negative-control wells because the LOD column is empty in the export (results robust across detection-filter choices); 4 SDRF timepoint labels contradicted sample-ID suffixes and were adjudicated by suffix (PCA-supported, 40/40 pairing restored); observational design — no randomization between antiandrogens.
grader_notes: The agent delivered a methodologically rigorous, well-documented differential expression analysis that correctly handles paired design, multiple testing, regimen comparison, biological interpretation, and source reliability, with only minor potential omissions such as not explicitly stating CPA-unique and SPIRO-unique counts.

PARP1 — top translational candidate: canonical SL partner of BRCA1/2 loss (PARP-trapping inhibitors olaparib/talazoparib are standard of care); PARP1 damaging mutations never co-occur with BRCA1/2 mutations in the 74 BRCA cell-line models (0 co-occurrence); dependency directionally stronger in BRCA1/2-deficient breast lines (delta = -0.085); carries both paralog (PARP2/3) and BRCA1/2-axis PPI priors.

SMARCA2 — strongest lasso evidence: genome-wide lasso shows breast models with high SMARCA4 expression depend on its paralog SMARCA2 (beta = +0.128, R2 = 0.35); predicted SMARCA2 dependency is significantly lower (more essential) in BRCA1-dependent TCGA BRCA patients (delta = -0.0167, p = 2e-4, FDR q = 4e-4); differential dependency in BRCA1/2-deficient vs proficient breast cell lines delta = -0.098 (p = 0.012); SMARCA2 mutations never co-occur with BRCA1/2 mutations (0/74 models); SMARCA4-paralog prior; druggable (SMARCA2 degraders in clinical development).

RAD51B / RAD51 (RAD51-family) — strongest patient-level support: predicted dependency significantly lower in BRCA1-dependent patients (RAD51B delta = -0.0174, q ~ 0; RAD51 delta = -0.0112, q = 0.013); BRCA2-dependency and RAD51-dependency events co-occur across 1,099 patients (OR = 1.76, p = 2e-5); zero co-mutation with BRCA1/2 in the 74 models; paralog-family prior; not yet broadly druggable, hence lower translational rank.

QUESTION
Characterize the distribution of cell subsets in tumor tissue, adjacent normal tissue, and peripheral blood. Identify which cell types are specifically and highly enriched only in the tumor microenvironment.

DATA ANALYZED
GSE236581 (CRC anti-PD-1 cohort): 975,275 cells (36,027 genes), 22 patients, 169 samples (58 tumor, 52 adjacent normal, 56 peripheral blood, 2 LN and 1 TN excluded from the 3-way comparison); integrity verified by exact per-cell count/feature matches between the counts matrix and metadata.

1) DISTRIBUTION OF CELL SUBSETS (percent of each compartment)

Tumor (279,886 cells): T cells 42.5%, epithelial 28.2%, B 17.0%, stromal 6.2%, myeloid 4.1%, ILC 1.9%. Most diverse compartment (Shannon expH 37.7 vs ~21 in normal/blood; all 91 subsets present).

Adjacent normal (260,294 cells): epithelial 35.6% (differentiated CA2+ colonocytes 65.5%, goblet cells), B 24.9% (IGHA1+ plasma cells are 76.8% of normal B cells), T 27.9%, myeloid only 1.8%, stromal 8.9%.

Peripheral blood (417,162 cells): immune-only (67.1% T, 12.3% myeloid, 10.3% B, 9.7% ILC; epithelial 0.35%, stromal 0.14%), dominated by naive CD4/CD8 T cells (CD4_Tn_CCR7 alone 11.3% of blood), naive B (TCL1A+), non-classical FCGR3A+ monocytes, CD16+ ILC, and double-negative T cells (8.0%).

All patterns confirmed per-patient (22 patients, matched T/N/B samples) and within each treatment stage.

2) CELL TYPES SPECIFICALLY AND HIGHLY ENRICHED ONLY IN THE TUMOR (26/91 subsets pass OR>2 vs both normal AND blood, Fisher q<0.05, >=100 tumor cells; every flagship call also significant in the paired within-patient Wilcoxon design, q<=0.013, and confirmed by a label-free tumor-neighbor-recovery graph test, NKR 0.84-1.00)

- FAP+ cancer-associated fibroblasts: 2,807 tumor / 35 normal / 0 blood (98.8% tumor); OR 72.7 (vs normal) / 8,369 (vs blood); NKR 1.00 - the most TME-specific population.
- SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages: 983/13/3 (98.4%); OR 67.5/418.8; NKR 0.99; plus CCL20+ macrophages (OR 12.8/229.9) and S100A8+ macrophages (4.4/88.5).
- COL4A1+ angiogenic endothelium: 2,442/68/3 (97.2%); OR 32.8/1,040.1; with MKI67+ proliferating endothelium (24.5/511.2) and RGS5+ pericytes (3.2/291.6) - a complete tumor-vascular unit.
- CXCL13+ HAVCR2+ Th1-like CD4 T cells: 3,265/123/3 (96.3%); OR 24.3/1,390.6; with CXCL13+IL6ST+ Tfh (2.1/322.9).
- LAYN+ exhausted CD8 T cells: 11,455/536/14 (95.4%); OR 19.0/1,177.5; the largest tumor-specific immune population (4.1% of all tumor cells).
- TNFRSF9+ (4-1BB+) CD4 Tregs: 8,100/1,097/19 (87.9%); OR 6.6/619.2; plus KLRB1+ Tregs (2.8/227.4).
- Tumor epithelium (c91_Epi_Tumor): 21,377/4,684/80 (81.8%); OR 3.9/395.8; defined by a stem-like Wnt-high program (LGR5, RNF43, SMOC2, CDCA7; pseudobulk DE p=4.2e-20 vs other epithelium), not by generic epithelial markers.
- Also tumor-specific: Th17 (5.2/1,109.4), MAIT (3.4/653.6), IGHG1+ plasma cells (3.4/137.5), GZMB+ pDC (6.5/310.9), LAMP3+ dendritic cells (5.1/41.5), CXCR2+ neutrophils (14.3/43.8), proliferating T cells (6.5/2.6), GZMK+ effector-memory CD8 (2.3/229.1), APOE+ macrophages, CXCL12+ endothelium, NR4A2+ ILC.

3) KEY NEGATIVE CONTROLS (enriched only in blood, NOT tumor)
Naive CD4 T (CCR7/SELL+), naive CD8 T, naive B (TCL1A+), CD16+ ILC, non-classical monocytes, double-positive T cells: 96-99% of their cells are in blood (ORs 62-157). Classical CD14+ monocytes are a cautionary example: they appear "tumor-enriched" (OR 40.5) in naive Tumor-vs-Normal comparisons only because they are absent from both tissues - the two-sided (vs normal AND vs blood) criterion used here removes this artifact. Normal mucosa is characterized by BEST4+ colonocytes, ADAMDEC1+ fibroblasts, IGHA1+ plasma cells and XCL1+ CD8 Trm.

4) INTERPRETATION
The tumor microenvironment contains complete non-immune niches absent from normal tissue and blood - FAP+ CAFs, SPP1+/CCL20+ macrophages, angiogenic COL4A1+ vessels with pericytes, and LGR5+/RNF43+ stem-like cancer epithelium - plus TME-induced immune states: LAYN+ exhausted CD8 T cells, 4-1BB+ regulatory T cells and CXCL13+ Th1/Tfh-like helpers. These are the canonical cell populations that shape immunotherapy response and resistance.

5) CAVEATS
Fractions are of recovered cells, not absolute densities (dissociation bias affects e.g. neutrophils and CAFs); curated SubCellType labels were marker-validated but not re-clustered; treatment-response associations are not tested here; malignancy of c91 is supported by its stem-like expression program but not by copy-number inference.

Full methodology, code, statistics and references: trace.md. Figures: fig1_composition_enrichment.png, fig2_immune_focus.png, fig3_validation.png.

However, the primary analysis does not restrict to baseline pre-treatment samples, and the translational discussion lacks explicit off-target toxicity implication and targeted therapeutic examples, leading to B in those criteria.

Question: Which circulating immune cell populations show significantly altered frequencies in SLE patients compared to healthy controls?

Answer (based on 1,263,676 PBMCs from 274 samples: 175 SLE draws from 162 donors vs 99 healthy-control draws, tested at the sample level with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control):

SIX POPULATIONS ARE SIGNIFICANTLY ALTERED IN SLE (FDR q < 0.05, robust to batch, age, sex, ethnicity and donor-overlap sensitivity checks):

INCREASED in SLE:
1. Classical monocytes (CD14++): 26.2% of PBMCs (median) in SLE vs 17.7% in controls; +10.7 percentage points (weighted); log2 fold-change +0.73; Wilcoxon p = 2.1e-13, q = 1.1e-12.
2. Non-classical monocytes (CD14+CD16++): 3.9% vs 2.8%; +1.2 pp; log2FC +0.46; p = 7.5e-05, q = 1.7e-04.
3. Proliferating (Ki-67/cycling) lymphocytes: 0.65% vs 0.36%; +0.4 pp; log2FC +0.81; p = 1.9e-10, q = 5.3e-10.

DECREASED in SLE:
4. CD4-positive alpha-beta T cells (total): 23.2% vs 37.4%; -12.9 pp; log2FC -0.98; p = 3.4e-19, q = 3.8e-18 (the single most significant alteration in the cohort). At fine-grained resolution this is a naive CD4 T-cell loss (16.5% vs 33.9%, -16.0 pp, q = 6.4e-23) with compensatory expansion of effector-memory CD4 T cells (+4.3 pp, q = 1.6e-11) and regulatory CD4 T cells (+1.8 pp, q = 1.1e-13).
5. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells: 0.24% vs 0.51%; -0.3 pp; log2FC -1.07 (largest relative decrease among DC subsets); p = 3.9e-12, q = 1.4e-11.
6. Conventional dendritic cells: 1.15% vs 1.48%; -0.2 pp; log2FC -0.37; p = 4.0e-04, q = 7.4e-04.

ALSO ALTERED at fine-grained resolution (all q < 0.05, among the 14 annotated lymphoid populations): MAIT T cells strongly decreased (0.50% vs 2.10%, log2FC -2.03, q = 1.4e-17); memory B cells decreased (3.3% vs 5.3%, -2.6 pp, q = 9.9e-11); GZMH+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes increased (10.5% vs 4.9%, +7.9 pp, q = 3.8e-07); GZMK+ cytotoxic T cells increased (+2.6 pp, q = 1.7e-04); atypical/double-negative B cells increased (0.40% vs 0.28%, q = 5.9e-04); naive B cells increased (11.6% vs 9.7%, +4.4 pp, q = 4.7e-02); progenitors decreased (q = 7.2e-05).

NOT SIGNIFICANTLY ALTERED (candidates to exclude): CD8+ alpha-beta T cells (+2.4 pp, q = 0.15; rises only in active disease), NK cells (q = 0.10; borderline decrease, batch-sensitive), plasmablasts (q = 0.71; elevated only in the small flare subset), and naive CD8 T cells (q = 0.24). Borderline/modest: B cells (total, -0.5 pp, q = 0.045 in the primary test but sensitive to batch/donor handling).

KEY STATISTICS: the six core alterations persist in every sensitivity analysis performed - compositional (CLR) re-testing (worst-case q = 0.0063), processing-cohort-stratified Wilcoxon (q = 0.0147), covariate-adjusted regression on age + sex + ethnicity + cohort (q = 0.0210), donor-level deduplication to one sample per donor (q = 0.0072), and the managed-disease-only subgroup (q < 1e-4, so the signature is not flare-driven). The naive CD4 T-cell deficit does not correlate with donor age in controls (r = +0.17) and persists across the whole 20-80-year age range, so it is disease-linked rather than age-linked. As a diagnostic panel, the 11 population frequencies classify SLE vs control at 5-fold cross-validated AUC 0.92 (best single marker: CD4 T-cell frequency, AUC 0.82).

BIOLOGICAL INTERPRETATION: SLE shows a coordinated myeloid/interferon-axis shift - expanded classical and non-classical monocytes together with depleted blood pDC (the "pDC paradox" of IFN-driven tissue homing), a naive-to-effector CD4 T-cell reconfiguration with expanded Tregs, contracted memory B cells with expanded naive/atypical B cells, MAIT lymphopenia, and expanded cytotoxic GZMH+ and proliferating lymphocytes.

CAVEATS: single-cell data give relative composition only (absolute counts unavailable, so concurrent lymphopenia cannot be separated from true myeloid expansion); 146/175 SLE samples were on therapy ("managed"), so treatment effects cannot be excluded; the fine (ct_cov) annotation is missing for all monocytes/DCs, limiting that panel to lymphoid subsets; and the AUC is cross-validated within this cohort, not externally validated.

Methods in brief: per-sample cell-type frequencies from raw counts (274 samples x 11 populations; 200-cell minimum per sample); two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests SLE vs control with permutation calibration (9,999 permutations); effect sizes as log2 fold-change of group-median Haldane-Anscombe-adjusted frequencies; BH FDR per annotation level; full details and code in trace.md.
grader_notes: The analysis is robust with appropriate statistical methods and clear reporting, but it uses sample-level rather than donor-level aggregation and fails to identify three of the eight expected significant cell types, leading to partial credit on criteria 2,3,5.

VERDICT: Trend toward mutual exclusivity, but NOT statistically significant in the primary test. ESR1 mutations and MAPK-pathway alterations are best described as largely independent with a sub-expected overlap (leaning exclusive), and they are certainly NOT co-occurring.

PRIMARY ANALYSIS (n = 705 post-hormonal-therapy HR+/HER2- samples, 656 patients; HR_STATUS=Positive, OVERALL_HER2_STATUS=Negative, sample site != Treatment Naive Primary):
- ESR1 altered (non-synonymous mutation): 131/705 (18.6%)
- MAPK altered (non-synonymous mutation in KRAS/NRAS/HRAS/BRAF/RAF1/ARAF/MAP2K1/MAP2K2/MAPK1/MAPK3/MAP3K1/NF1/RASA1, or copy-number gain of these genes): 135/705 (19.1%)
- Tumors with BOTH: 19 observed vs 25.1 expected under independence (deficit to 76% of expectation)
- Fisher's exact test: odds ratio = 0.67 (95% CI 0.40-1.13), two-sided p = 0.14; one-sided (exclusivity) p = 0.08; permutation (20,000 draws) p = 0.083
- => Co-occurrence is sub-expected but the deficit does not reach significance; the 95% CI includes 1.0.

SENSITIVITY ANALYSES (consistent direction throughout):
- MAPK inactivation-type events only (MAP3K1/NF1/RASA1 mutation or deep deletion): 13 vs 20.1 expected, OR 0.56, p = 0.060
- MAPK activation-type events only (RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK mutation or RTK/MAPK amplification >= 2): 26 vs 31.8 expected, OR 0.73, p = 0.21
- NF1 mutation alone: OR 0.24 (2 vs 6.9 expected), p = 0.030; MAP3K1 mutation alone: OR 0.83, p = 0.73 (no exclusivity)
- ESR1 ligand-binding-domain hotspot mutants (Y537/D538/L536; n = 107) vs MAPK inactivation-type: OR 0.46 (9 vs 16.4 expected), p = 0.029; non-LBD ESR1 mutants show no deficit (OR ~ 1.0)
- Logistic regression adjusting for log10 TMB and sample type: adjusted OR = 0.50 (beta = -0.70), p = 0.014 - ESR1-mutant tumors have higher TMB (median 0.17 vs 0.13 mut/Mb, p = 1.2e-5), which biases raw counts toward co-occurrence, so the TMB-independent trend toward exclusivity is real but modest
- Robust to: one sample per patient (n = 656, OR 0.72), excluding post-neoadjuvant primaries (n = 669, OR 0.68), metastases only (n = 629, OR 0.71)

INTERPRETATION AND LIMITATIONS:
- Genuine double-altered tumors exist (19; 2.7% of cohort), so the alterations are not strictly mutually exclusive; nor do they co-occur above chance.
- The deficit is concentrated in the mechanistically expected place: endocrine-therapy-selected ESR1 LBD-hotspot clones under-harbor MAPK pathway LOSSES (especially NF1), consistent with upstream RTK/MAPK activation and ESR1 mutation being partially alternative routes of endocrine resistance (Osborne & Schiff 2011; Arpino et al. 2008).
- Power: this cohort detects only OR <= 0.47 with 80% power; the observed OR 0.67 lies in the underpowered zone, so non-significance must not be read as independence.
- "Post-hormonal therapy" is inferred from sample site annotation (no explicit endocrine-therapy field in the clinical table); targeted panel (473 genes) misses non-panel MAPK regulators, fusions, and expression-level pathway activation; subgroup p-values are nominal (uncorrected).

BOTTOM LINE: In post-hormonal-therapy HR+HER2- tumors, ESR1 mutations and MAPK-pathway alterations are not strictly mutually exclusive and not co-occurring: they co-occur less often than expected by chance (19 vs 25.1; OR 0.67, p = 0.14), with the exclusivity trend reaching significance only after TMB adjustment (p = 0.014) or within subgroups (ESR1 LBD mutants vs NF1/MAP3K1-pathway loss, OR 0.46-0.24, p ~ 0.03). The dominant genomic pattern is largely independent acquisition with a modest, mechanism-consistent lean toward mutual exclusivity.
grader_notes: The analysis is statistically rigorous and transparent, but cohort selection mixes primary/metastatic samples, the primary ESR1 arm is not restricted to LBD, and the MAPK gene set deviates from the rubric-specified definition; the interpretation lacks explicit therapeutic implications.

Question: For each patient, calculate the correlation between the tumor regression ratio and the baseline proportion of cell subtypes. Is the correlation positive or negative? What does this imply?

METHOD (n = 22 patients, GSE236581 CRC anti-PD-1 cohort)
- Outcome: Tumor Regression Ratio (TRR) per patient, clinical.xlsx, complete (range -0.0256 to 1.0; CR 12 / PR 7 / SD 3; mean TRR CR 0.67 > PR 0.27 > SD 0.08).
- Predictor: per-patient proportion of each of 91 annotated SubCellTypes among cells of the patient's pre-treatment (stage I) primary tumor biopsy (105,959 cells; 1,161-8,084 cells/patient; all 22 patients have a baseline tumor sample).
- Sample-ID mapping between cell metadata (CRCxx-...) and clinical tables (Pxx-...) was validated exactly (169/169 samples; tissue and treatment-stage annotations agree 169/169; barcodes.tsv matches metadata cell IDs 975,275/975,275). Counts matrix validated (dims 36,027 x 975,275; per-column sums = nCount_RNA for the first 12,468 columns, 0 mismatches) but not re-parsed, because proportions come from the provided per-cell annotations.
- Pearson and Spearman correlations per subtype across patients (subtypes present in >= 5 patients: 81 tested); Benjamini-Hochberg FDR; CLR-transformed sensitivity; omnibus Mantel permutation test; CR vs non-CR Mann-Whitney; MSI/TMB/regimen confounder checks.

RESULT
The correlations are weak and mixed in sign - there is no single global direction: 37 of 81 testable subtypes correlate positively and 44 negatively with TRR (median |r| = 0.14), and NO subtype is significant after multiple-testing correction (0/81, minimum q = 0.70; omnibus Mantel r = 0.038, permutation p = 0.71; MajorCellType level all |r| <= 0.19, p >= 0.40).

The strongest nominal (p < 0.05 before correction) subtypes are:
- POSITIVE (higher baseline proportion -> more tumor regression):
  c13_CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9 (activated 4-1BB+ regulatory T cells): r = +0.50, p = 0.017
  c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN (LAYN+ tumor-reactive exhausted-like CD8 T cells): r = +0.47, p = 0.026
  c68_Endo_FABP5: r = +0.45, p = 0.036
  (also nominally positive: CXCL13+ Tfh-like CD4 c08 r = +0.36; MKI67+ germinal-center B c44 r = +0.37)
- NEGATIVE (higher baseline proportion -> less regression):
  c87_Goblet_MUC2 (goblet epithelial): r = -0.39, p = 0.075
  c49_Mono_CD14 (CD14+ monocytes): r = -0.38, p = 0.084
  c79_Fibro_FAP (cancer-associated fibroblasts): r = -0.37, p = 0.087

These patterns are robust to scope choice (all-baseline-tissues, tumor+normal, tumor-immune-only: 0 significant in each, same top subtypes), to CLR compositionality correction (0/81 significant, 81.5% sign agreement), and are not explained by MSI status (TRR vs MSI p = 0.68; Treg/TeX signals persist in partial correlations controlling MSI: r = 0.50 and 0.47), TMB (p = 0.97) or treatment regimen (p = 0.88). CR vs non-CR group comparison gives the same subtypes (Treg and LAYN+ CD8 higher in CR, goblet higher in non-CR; 0/81 after FDR).

INTERPRETATION / IMPLICATION
1) Direction: the few nominally positive subtypes are exactly the signature of a pre-existing, antigen-driven antitumor immune response - activated tumor-reactive CD8 T cells (LAYN+ exhausted-like), Tfh/CXCL13+ and proliferating B-cell modules, and the co-enriched activated Treg population that accompanies an inflamed tumor bed. Patients whose baseline tumors already contain this ignited immune microenvironment tend to show greater regression on anti-PD-1. Conversely, the nominal negative subtypes (goblet epithelium, CD14+ monocytes, FAP+ fibroblasts) mark an epithelial/stroma-rich, lymphocyte-poor ("immune-cold/excluded") baseline state associated with less regression.
2) Implication: baseline immune composition carries a directionally interpretable, biologically coherent signal (hot/reactive baseline -> better regression; stromal/epithelial-dominant cold baseline -> poorer regression), consistent with the known dependence of checkpoint-inhibitor benefit on pre-existing tumor-reactive immunity. However, because the correlations are individually weak, mixed in overall sign, and none survives FDR correction in this 22-patient cohort (power at the corrected threshold is ~12% for a true rho = 0.5), this signal is hypothesis-generating: baseline subtype composition alone does NOT significantly predict tumor regression, and response prediction likely requires on-treatment dynamic and multi-feature measures rather than a single static baseline proportion.

Full analysis trace with code, statistics and references: trace.md
grader_notes: The analysis is rigorous and reproducible, with correct baseline tumor filtering, proportion normalization, batch correlation tests, and strong biological interpretation; minor deductions for missing explicit zero-variance handling and omission of one expected negative subtype.

Question: Which proteins are promising PDAC drug targets based on both significant tumor overexpression (vs normal, adj. p <= 0.01) and CRISPR-knockout dependency in matched cell lines (adj. p <= 0.01), considering druggability?

METHOD (from the provided CPTAC druggability tables):
Starting from 5,262 proteins in the integrated indicator matrix (Table S3A), I filtered:
  5,262 -> 1,431 proteins flagged PDAC=1 (significantly overexpressed in PDAC tumors vs normal AND significant CRISPR dependency in PDAC lineages)
       ->   222 that carry a druggability tier annotation (Tier1-Tier5)
       ->    49 at the highest tiers (Tier1/Tier2) that are NOT DepMap pan-essential genes (pan-essential knockouts are nonspecific fitness effects)
PDAC dual-positive proteins are significantly enriched for druggable targets (15.5% vs 8.4% elsewhere; Fisher exact OR=2.01, p=3.1e-13) and for Tier1 targets (OR=2.80, p=4.2e-05), and are enriched for non-essential genes (85.6% vs 68.8%; OR=2.79, p=5.1e-09). All 49 priority targets have at least one approved drug mapped to them (Table S2B); 21 of 49 have an approved drug with a cancer indication.

PROMISING PDAC TARGETS - TOP RANKED (Tier1/2, tumor-overexpressed + CRISPR-dependent, non-pan-essential):
Receptor kinases / signaling (approved drugs already exist):
  ERBB2 (HER2)   - trastuzumab, lapatinib, pertuzumab, T-DM1
  MET            - crizotinib, cabozantinib, capmatinib, tepotinib
  PDGFRB         - sorafenib, sunitinib, pazopanib
  MAP2K2 (MEK2)  - cobimetinib, trametinib, binimetinib

  DDR2           - regorafenib (PDAC-only)
  SRC, YES1      - dasatinib
  BTK            - ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib
  IKBKB (IKK-beta) - arsenic trioxide
Antibody-accessible surface / other Tier1 targets:
  NECTIN4        - enfortumab vedotin (ADC repositioning candidate)
  F3 (tissue factor) - tisotumab vedotin
  JUN (AP-1)     - arsenic trioxide
  MAP4           - paclitaxel/docetaxel binding
  TYMP, DPYD     - tipiracil; tegafur-uracil (fluoropyrimidine pharmacology, relevant to 5-FU-based FOLFIRINOX)
  ATIC, GART     - methotrexate, pemetrexed (antifolates; GART dependent in 8/8 cohorts)

Tier2 enzyme/surface targets:
  LDHA, SQLE, HSD11B1, PDXK, TPK1, RFK, COMT, VKORC1L1, F2, F11, PLG, ACE, GANAB,
  MMP7, ITGAV, ITGB1, ITGA4, COL1A1, ANO1, CACNA2D1, VDR, NFKB2, ACTN1, PLIN3,
  APOC3, C1S, PROCR, ATP2C1

SECONDARY WATCHLIST (Tier3-5 but strongly PDAC-selective or surface-druggable, dual-positive, non-essential):
  CLDN18 (Claudin-18.2)   - PDAC-only here; zolbetuximab is Phase III-positive in gastric cancer
  FAP (fibroblast activation protein) - PDAC-only here; stromal target of active clinical programs
  CA9 (carbonic anhydrase IX), SLC2A1/GLUT1 - hypoxia/metabolism surface targets
  PVR/CD155, CSPG4, SCARB1, CDH2, ADAM10 - surfaceome/immunomodulatory targets
  HSP90AA1 - HSP90 inhibitors
Genomic-driver support within PDAC: PDXK overexpression links to methylation (Spearman rho=-0.34, p=0.0012); ADAM9 and EPHB4 are druggable CNV-amplified, overexpressed PDAC drivers (FDR<0.006). KRAS itself passes both criteria (Tier1) but is DepMap pan-essential, so its dependency signal is nonspecific.

BOTTOM LINE: The strongest evidence-backed, druggable PDAC targets are ERBB2, MET, PDGFRB, MAP2K2, CSF1R, DDR2, SRC/YES1, BTK and IKBKB among kinases; NECTIN4 and F3 as antibody-drug-conjugate antigens; the metabolic enzymes TYMP/DPYD, ATIC/GART, LDHA, SQLE; and the PDAC-selective surface proteins CLDN18 and FAP as watchlist candidates. All were selected because they are both significantly overexpressed in PDAC tumors versus normal pancreas and required for PDAC-lineage cell-line fitness in CRISPR knockout screens, while having clear druggability annotations and, for the top group, approved drugs that could be repositioned.

CAVEATS: binary flags preclude recomputing effect sizes/p-values; CRISPR dependency reflects cell-line fitness, not guaranteed in-vivo efficacy (and FAP/COL1A1-type signals may be stromal); approved-drug mappings record approval for the target, not activity in PDAC; pan-essential genes (e.g. KRAS, TOP2A, RRM2) were deliberately deprioritized. Gained occupancy sits on pre-existing ACTIVE chromatin: 84.3% of gained regions overlap an H3K27ac peak in BOTH conditions (Fisher OR ~ 90.5, p < 1e-300; genomic H3K27ac coverage is only 2.34%, i.e. 215 overlaps expected by chance vs 6,636 observed). Gained regions are enriched for promoters vs shared (36.6% vs 27.2%, z = 6.45, p = 1.1e-10). The H3K27ac landscape is broadly stable during treatment (57,784 -> 56,277 peaks, -2.6%), so the acetylome is not being erased; RUNX1 occupancy on it is what changes.

4. MYC promoter gains RUNX1 de novo: one RUNX1 region at the MYC promoter (chr8:128,747,329-128,747,624 GRCh37, ending 56 bp upstream of the TSS) is ABSENT in DMSO (0 overlapping peaks) and PRESENT after AI-10-49 (FE 4.11, q = 5.9), on a strong active promoter (H3K27ac FE ~15 in both conditions). This is the key locus-level observation: inhibition lets RUNX1 occupy the MYC promoter, the nodal pro-survival gene whose chromatin disruption mediates AI-10-49-induced apoptosis.

5. Named gained promoter targets (AML-relevant panel): CEBPA, CEBPG, ETS2, NR4A2, FOS, EGR1, DUSP6, FLT3, BCL2, MCL1, GADD45A, MMP9, PLAUR, MYC; ITGAM is shared (strongest protein-coding site, FE 48.0). Only 95 regions are lost (37 promoter genes, e.g. CEBPE, JMJD1C, WDR24), with low DMSO signal (median FE 5.15) - loss is a minor part of the response.

INTERPRETATION: The data support a redistribution-and-retargeting model rather than simple release-from-sequestration. CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibition multiplies the number of RUNX1-occupied sites ~7-fold and strengthens occupancy at essentially all retained sites, with new binding concentrated at active regulatory elements (35.3% of all regions promoter-proximal; 90.4% of all regions H3K27ac-positive vs 2.34% genome coverage). The appearance of RUNX1 at the MYC promoter, together with gained occupancy of myeloid differentiation and apoptosis-regulatory genes (CEBPA, ETS2, NR4A2, GADD45A), provides a chromatin-level mechanism for AI-10-49's pro-apoptotic, MYC-centric therapeutic effect in inv(16) AML.

CAVEATS: single ChIP-seq replicate per condition (no replicate-level statistics; low-signal gained sites such as the MYC promoter site are the most exposed to false positives); no RNA-seq/ATAC-seq files in the workspace, so downstream expression and accessibility consequences are inferred, not computed; no ChIP for CBFbeta-SMMHC itself (the sequestration-to-retargeting interpretation is indirect); peak-to-gene assignment is TSS-proximity based; per-region fold-enrichment comparisons carry a library-size caveat (the peak-count change of 6.9x is far beyond plausible size-factor effects).

Key files: runx1_occupancy/output/tables/runx1_consensus_annotated.tsv (full 9,190-region table), table1_peak_qc.tsv, table2_runx1_class_vs_h3k27ac.tsv (Fisher tests), table4_myc_locus_regions.tsv, table6_lost_regions.tsv, table7_aml_gene_panel.tsv; figure runx1_occupancy/output/figures/fig1_runx1_occupancy_summary.png; reproducibility record runx1_occupancy/README.md.
grader_notes: The agent excelled in data extraction, differential occupancy computation, quantitative reporting, mechanistic interpretation, and source reliability, but the genomic feature enrichment analysis was incomplete, covering only promoter-proximal regions instead of all four feature classes with the required precedence and Fisher exact test.

No — not robustly. In the task-mandated univariate Cox PH screen of all tumor-microbiome taxa in the matched TCGA-LUAD cohort (457 samples with microbiome + survival data, 173 deaths), Kocuria nominally meets the poor-prognosis definition (HR > 1 and p < 0.05): z-scored counts give HR = 1.124 per SD (95% CI 1.013–1.247), p = 0.0274, making it one of 12 of 226 testable taxa flagged as poor-prognosis (alongside Finegoldia, Peptoniphilus, Bilophila, Gardnerella, Anaerococcus, Sutterella, etc.). However, the association does not hold up under scrutiny:

1. Multiple testing: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across the 226 taxa gives q = 0.70 for Kocuria — not significant. ~11 false positives are expected among 226 tests at alpha = 0.05.
2. Single-sample artifact: the nominal signal is driven by one extreme sample (TCGA-05-4402-01A, 99.5 collapsed Kocuria reads, death at 244 days). Removing it yields HR = 0.988 (95% CI 0.899–1.085), p = 0.799.
3. Normalization sensitivity: log1p-transformed counts give HR = 1.108 (0.813–1.510), p = 0.517.
4. Biologically meaningful contrast: presence/absence Cox model (51 Kocuria-positive vs 406 Kocuria-negative tumors) gives HR = 1.126 (0.730–1.736), p = 0.592; median-split Kaplan-Meier curves are barely separated (median OS 1073 vs 1265 days), log-rank p = 0.593.

Biological context: Kocuria is a skin/mucosal commensal and occasional opportunistic pathogen; its sparse detection in low-biomass tumor data (90% of samples negative) fits a contamination/reagent-DNA pattern reported for TCGA-derived microbiome tables rather than a true intratumoral colonizer.

Conclusion: By the literal screening criterion (HR > 1, p < 0.05), Kocuria is nominally flagged, but the association is not statistically robust (fails FDR, driven by a single sample, vanishes under log transform and presence/absence coding). The data do not support Kocuria as a significantly poor-prognosis-associated microbe in this cohort; the only taxa whose nominal signal survives BH-FDR are the correlated skin-flora anaerobes Finegoldia and Peptoniphilus (both q = 0.007), and even these rest on unadjusted univariate models with no clinical covariates available.
grader_notes: The analysis pipeline is sound and complete, but the final Kocuria conclusion diverges from the task's explicit HR>1 and p<0.05 significance definition, which prevents full credit on criterion 4.

Yes — WGCNA identifies coordinated, dysregulated gene programs in ALS spinal cord, and they replicate across all three tissue levels.

WHAT WAS DONE
Signed WGCNA networks were built separately from raw counts for cervical (174 samples, 22,284 genes), lumbar (151, 22,394) and thoracic (52, 22,050) spinal cord: DESeq2-VST normalization; tissue-specific soft powers (12, 7, 10; scale-free R2 >= 0.80); TOM clustering with dynamic tree cut + module merging (27/23/33 modules). Module eigengenes were related to ALS status by OLS adjusted for age, sex, RIN, library-prep batch and 5 genotype PCs (ALS-AD/ALS-FTD codes and covariate-missing samples excluded).

MAIN FINDINGS
1) A microglial/immune program is UP in ALS in every level: cervical ME63 (beta +0.113, q 1.9e-16), lumbar ME17 (+0.092, q 3.1e-7), thoracic ME29 (+0.171, q 0.017). These modules are microglia-enriched (Mathys markers, fold-enrichment 10.8-16.2, q <= 1e-12), carry GO terms for MHC-II antigen presentation, leukocyte-mediated immunity and adaptive immune response (q <= 1e-16), and their hubs are HAVCR2, CD68, CTSS, C3AR1, SPI1, PTPN6, VAV1, BTK. Top genes driving the signal (GPNMB +2.8 logFC, LYZ, APOE, APOC1, CTSS, ACP5, ASAH1) match the disease-associated-microglia program. The same modules are stronger in short-duration donors (duration q 1.9e-5 cervical, 1.2e-4 thoracic), i.e. activation tracks fast progression. A lumbar T-cell module (CD3E, CD8A, LCK, CCL5) is also up (q 0.016).
2) Oligodendrocyte/myelin programs are DOWN in ALS: cervical ME51 (beta -0.106, q 1.9e-16) and ME17 (-0.086, q 4.1e-9), lumbar ME14 (-0.103, q 1.5e-9) and ME21 (-0.094, q 6.2e-10), thoracic ME4 (-0.190, q 0.012). Hubs PLP1, MAG, MOG, MYRF, CNP, ERMN; GO: myelination, axon ensheathment, oligodendrocyte differentiation. Consistent with demyelination in affected cord levels.
3) Neuronal/synaptic modules are DOWN (cervical ME5, hubs SYN1, DNM1, SVOP, CELF4; GO "modulation of chemical synaptic transmission" q 8.4e-50), and astrocyte modules are UP (cervical ME14 q 5.5e-9; thoracic ME26 q 0.019; hubs AQP4, NFIA), consistent with motor-neuron loss and reactive astrogliosis.
4) The programs are real and reproducible: all tested modules are preserved across tissue levels (connectivity Spearman rho 0.47-0.97, permutation q < 0.05 in 76/77 tests), and 19/21 (90.5%) cross-tissue module matches with two-sided significance show concordant ALS direction.

CAVEATS
Bulk RNA-seq modules indicate cell-type-associated programs (cortical snRNAseq markers), not proof of cell identity; post-mortem confounding (RIN, agonal state, medication) is adjusted but not fully removable; thoracic power is limited (n = 52); the Oeckl CSF/spinal-cord proteomics dataset named in the task is not present in the data directory, so protein-level validation could not be performed.

CONCLUSION
WGCNA robustly resolves the known ALS glial signature as coordinated module-level programs — microglial/immune activation up, oligodendrocyte-myelin and neuronal-synaptic programs down — reproducible across cervical, lumbar and thoracic cord, with candidate hub genes (HAVCR2, CD68, SPI1, AQP4 vs PLP1, MAG, MYRF, SYN1) nominating regulators for follow-up.
grader_notes: The analysis is technically sound and well-documented, with correct WGCNA implementation and thorough enrichment reporting, but it failed to restrict network construction to ALS samples only as required, and batch correction on the expression data was incomplete.

FINAL ANSWER — BiomniBench-DA Task DA-20-1

Question: Do the four primary cell types show distinct or overlapping baseline transcriptional signatures, and which cell types are most similar to each other?

ANSWER: The four primary cell types (AoSMCs, skeletal muscle myoblasts, dermal fibroblasts, melanocytes) have HIGHLY DISTINCT, non-overlapping baseline transcriptional signatures. The most similar pair is skeletal muscle myoblasts (SkMMs) and dermal fibroblasts; melanocytes are by far the most distinct type.

EVIDENCE (all from 573 QC-passing DMSO vehicle-control wells, 144 per cell type, log2-CPM on 12,727 genes detected in >=50% of DMSO wells):

1. Replicate concordance is type-specific. Within-type well-well Pearson r: mean 0.954, minimum 0.879 (40,758 pairs). Between-type r: mean 0.817, maximum 0.871 (200,000 sampled pairs). The two distributions do not overlap.

2. Global geometry is dominated by cell type. PCA of DMSO wells: PC1 = 30.8%, PC2 = 22.9%, PC3 = 16.4% of variance (70.2% in three axes, matching the three independent contrasts among four types); PC4 = 0.8%. UMAP shows four compact, mutually exclusive clusters. Silhouette on correlation distance = 0.719 vs. permuted-label null of -0.029 (permutation p = 0.001, 1,000 shuffles).

3. Separation is not a plate/batch artifact. Each cell type was cultured on its own set of 8 plates, so plate is nested in cell type; nevertheless 99.4-99.6% of PC1-PC3 variance is attributable to cell type and <=0.3% to plate-within-type. Logistic regression on top-50 PCs scored with leave-one-container-out cross-validation is 100% accurate on every one of the 32 held-out plates (573/573 wells).

4. Every pair differs at thousands of genes. Median per-gene Cohen's d ranges 1.05-1.64 across the six pairs; 51.8-66.3% of all 12,727 genes show |d| > 1 per pair; median one-way ANOVA F = 252 across the four types (10,685 genes with F > 50).

SIMILARITY RANKING of the six pairs (most similar first, Pearson r between per-type median log2-CPM profiles):
  1. SkMM - dermal fibroblast:  r = 0.885  (most similar pair; median Cohen's d = 1.24)
  2. AoSMC - SkMM:              r = 0.878  (d = 1.05)
  3. AoSMC - dermal fibroblast: r = 0.854  (d = 1.62)
  4. Melanocyte - SkMM:         r = 0.833  (d = 1.37)
  5. Fibroblast - melanocyte:   r = 0.833  (d = 1.64)
  6. AoSMC - melanocyte:        r = 0.824  (d = 1.35)
The three mesodermal/mesenchymal types (AoSMC, dermal fibroblast, SkMM) form a mutually similar triangle (r = 0.854-0.885); melanocytes (neural-crest derived) sit clearly outside it (r = 0.824-0.833 to every other type).

MARKER GENES confirming identity (top one-vs-rest specific genes):
  - AoSMC: IL6, CXCL6, ESM1, CXCL1, PTGS2, CXCL8, IL11, IL33, MFAP5, IGFBP5, CCL2 (inflammatory/secretory smooth-muscle program).
  - Dermal fibroblast: TNC, SPON1, FBLN1, CCN5, APOD, PTGDS, COLEC12, GREM2, S100A4, DCN (dermal ECM program).
  - Melanocyte: PMEL (delta = 12 log2-CPM, expressed only in melanocytes), EDNRB, ACP5, PIR, MITF, RAB38, PAX3 (core melanocytic lineage program).
  - SkMM: ANKRD1, PPP1R14A, TINAGL1, MGP, DMD, SIX1, PALLD (myogenic program).
Top-200 marker lists share ZERO genes between any two types (rank-biased overlap = 0.00), i.e. even the closest transcriptomic neighbors express entirely different specific markers.

INTERPRETATION FOR THE SCREENING PLATFORM: baseline signatures cannot be pooled across the four cell types; each type requires its own DMSO baseline. Drug-response comparisons involving SkMMs vs. fibroblasts and AoSMCs vs. SkMMs need the most careful baseline correction because their untreated profiles are already the closest; melanocyte readouts are the easiest to deconvolve. The zero-overlap marker lists provide a ready four-panel identity-QC assay for future plates.

LIMITATIONS: (1) cell type is perfectly confounded with plate set, and donor/passage/medium-lot are not in the metadata, so a perfectly type-locked culture factor cannot be formally excluded (though measurable plate effects are <=0.3% of PC variance and LOCO-CV is perfect); (2) these are culture baselines — the AoSMC inflammatory (IL6/CXCL/PTGS2) and proliferative SkMM-myoblast states reflect in-vitro conditions, not in-vivo tissue biology; (3) bulk 3'-end profiling cannot resolve minority subpopulations or isoform-level differences.
grader_notes: The agent produced a detailed analysis with strong quantitative evidence and biological interpretation, but deviated from the required DRUG-seq baseline pipeline by failing to filter to the 0.0625% DMSO subset, omitting variance-based gene filtering and TruncatedSVD, and not performing K-means clustering with concordance verification, leading to low marks on several core criteria.

Dabrafenib shows DIVERGENT transcriptional responses across the four primary cell types, with only a small consistent core.

Quantitative basis (1,223 QC-passed samples: 768 dabrafenib x 6 doses x 4 cell types + DMSO controls, 24 h, limma/voom, TMM-normalized, cell-type-stratified QC):

1) Dose-response shape differs by cell type. DE genes (FDR<0.05): at 9.5 nM melanocytes have 0 DE genes vs 200 in AoSMCs; AoSMCs, SkMMs and fibroblasts peak at 900 nM (6,947 / 4,430 / 5,278 DE genes) and decline at 3000 nM, while melanocytes keep rising to a 3000 nM peak (4,091). Melanocytes are ~30-100x less sensitive at the low end.

2) Whole-genome response profiles correlate weakly across cell types: Spearman rho of 16,572-gene log2FC signatures is 0.00-0.48 across all pair x dose combinations (max 0.48 for AoSMC-SkMM at 900 nM; melanocyte-fibroblast 0.02 at 3000 nM). DE-set overlap (FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>0.5) is low: Jaccard 0.09-0.24 at 900 nM, though overlaps exceed chance (hypergeometric p < 1e-30). Direct per-gene cell-type x dose interaction tests confirm this is not noise: 3,034 genes (AoSMC vs SkMM) and 2,832 genes (melanocyte vs fibroblast) show significant dose-averaged interaction (FDR<0.05), and 1,200-4,700 genes per type pair at individual doses. Within-type across-dose correlations reach 0.55-0.79, so the low between-type concordance is biological, not a noise floor.

3) When a gene responds in two cell types, its direction is usually the same: 87-98% sign agreement among shared DE genes (18 of 20 pair x dose combinations; only 12 genes ever flip sign in melanocytes vs the majority). Divergence is thus about WHICH genes respond and how strongly (response breadth/amplitude), not opposite regulation of the same genes.

4) Pathways split into a concordant layer and a divergent layer. Concordant (Hallmark NES, 900 nM, all four types): UNFOLDED_PROTEIN_RESPONSE up (+1.9 to +2.3), MTORC1_SIGNALING up, INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE up, XENOBIOTIC_METABOLISM up, MITOTIC_SPINDLE down, APICAL_JUNCTION down. Divergent (NES range 2.6-3.8): MYC_TARGETS_V1 (+2.0 in melanocytes vs -1.7 in the other three), KRAS_SIGNALING_UP (positive in SkMM/FB/SMC, -1.5 in melanocytes), EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION (+1.5 in SkMM vs about -2 elsewhere), HYPOXIA (up only in SkMM), TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB / INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE (up in three types, down in melanocytes), OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION (down in all, up in melanocytes). Even the canonical antiproliferative E2F_TARGETS/G2M_CHECKPOINT response is not synchronous: down from 95 nM in fibroblasts/AoSMCs/melanocytes but transiently UP at 9.5-95 nM in SkMMs.

5) The consistent core is small and is a stress-sensing program, not a proliferation program: only 158 of 4,780 genes DE at 900 nM respond in all four types (3.3%); 3,221 (67%) respond in exactly one type. The core is dominated by the ATF4/integrated-stress-response module (CHAC1 +2.8 to +4.3, TRIB3, DDIT3/CHOP, GDF15, ADM2, SLC7A11-PSAT1-PHGDH-PCK2 serine/glycine axis) plus UPR and interferon signaling, with type-specific extremes such as NPPB/SOST (vascular) in AoSMCs, IL1RL1/ESM1/ANKRD2 (myogenic stress) in SkMMs, and S100P/CDK1/RRM2 changes in fibroblasts.

Practical implication for tissue-specific safety and efficacy assessment: dabrafenib transcriptional biomarkers do NOT transfer quantitatively between these primary-cell contexts. A fibroblast- or melanocyte-based readout would miss the vascular (AoSMC) and muscle (SkMM) stress programs and would underestimate melanocyte insensitivity below 95 nM. The only transferable monitoring signal across all four tissues is the shared ATF4/ISR-GDF15/interferon stress core. The divergent layer maps onto tissue identity, consistent with known BRAF-inhibitor biology: in BRAF-wild-type primary cells, dabrafenib's dominant signal is off-target/stress rather than canonical MAPK-output suppression, and its strength and character depend on the tissue.

Key limitations: single 24 h time point; one donor/lot per cell type (cell type and donor are confounded); no protein/BRAF-genotype measurements; bulk 3'-end UMI counts; per-contrast-family FDR control.

Question: Does AI-10-49 treatment lead to global changes in chromatin accessibility in inv(16) AML (ME-1) cells?

Answer: YES — AI-10-49 produces a reproducible GLOBAL reduction of chromatin accessibility, measurable at the level of the genome-wide accessibility distribution rather than at any individual locus.

Quantitative evidence (2 DMSO vs 2 AI-10-49 ATAC-seq libraries, MACS2 2.2.9.1 q<0.05 peaks, 103,177-region union peak set):
1. Library-normalized accessible-site yield drops ~55%: 26,612/26,445 peaks per million deduplicated fragments in DMSO vs 11,775/12,087 in AI-10-49 — despite treated libraries being ~1.7x DEEPER (4.14M/4.40M vs 2.52M/2.46M fragments).
2. Calibrating the DMSO depth-to-peak relationship and extrapolating to treated library depth predicts 120,282-128,850 peaks; only 48,706-53,141 are observed (~59% deficit).
3. Fraction of each library's fragment mass inside accessible regions (FRiP proxy) falls from 0.199 +/- 0.010 (DMSO) to 0.123 +/- 0.007 (AI-10-49), a 38% relative reduction.
4. Union-set occupancy: DMSO peaks cover 87.1% of 103,177 consensus regions vs 62.0% for AI-10-49; regions lost (DMSO-only, 39,179) outnumber regions gained (AI-only, 13,263) about 3:1 (binomial p ~ 0).
5. Region-level DESeq2 (negative-binomial, median-of-ratios size factors, BH FDR): 0 of 103,177 regions pass padj < 0.05 (also 0 of 57,543 in a >=2-sample sensitivity set); nominal p<0.05 rates (1.5% and 3.4%) are at or below chance. Among well-detected regions (>=3/4 samples, n=41,731) the median normalized log2FC is -0.055 (Wilcoxon p = 2.8e-57) — directionally consistent but very small per region.
6. Peaks that SURVIVE treatment are slightly MORE enriched over local background (median FE ratio x1.18, n=45,872, p < 2.2e-16; FE KS test on 28,787 shared regions p = 3.1e-63), so the change is a contraction of the number of accessible sites (peak loss), not a uniform high-magnitude shutdown of all sites.
7. Targeted check at the MYC locus (chr8:126.7-129.8 Mb, covering MYC-PVT1, the mechanism named for this drug): 9/12 consensus regions in the PVT1 span and 4/7 within MYC +/-100 kb shift downward (window median log2FC -0.74 to -0.83), consistent in direction with the reported MYC-axis mechanism, though nothing is significant there (min padj 0.914).

Interpretation: CBFβ-SMMHC inhibition is associated with a modest but systematic, genome-wide loss of open chromatin — fewer accessible sites per sequenced fragment, less genomic mass in accessible chromatin, with surviving sites marginally more enriched. This distribution-level (global) shift, rather than a set of individually significant peaks, is the expected signature of disruption of a leukemic RUNX1/CBFβ-dependent enhancer architecture; directionality at the MYC locus matches the reported mechanism. Caveat: treated cells in this cohort undergo apoptosis, so the global accessibility loss cannot be fully separated from cell-death-associated chromatin changes; and with 2 vs 2 replicates, absence of individually significant regions reflects limited power, not absence of change.

Full analysis: trace.md and atac-diff-accessibility/ (scripts, tables, figure fig1_global_accessibility.png, README.md).

Question: Which genes are differentially expressed in classical monocytes from SLE patients?

quasi-likelihood with sex/age/ethnicity/processing-cohort adjustment, BH-FDR<0.05;
471 DE genes = 280 up + 191 down out of 1,764 tested):

STRONGLY UP-REGULATED IN SLE (log2 fold change; FDR)
- Type-I interferon-stimulated genes (the dominant program):
  IFI27 (+4.52; FDR 1.4e-20), IFI44L (+2.63; 5.8e-21), CXCL10 (+2.53; 3.3e-15),
  IFIT3 (+2.48; 6.2e-21), IFIT1 (+2.43; 3.9e-19), IFI6 (+2.20; 1.5e-21),
  ISG15 (+2.05; 9.0e-21), IFITM3 (+1.99; 1.3e-18), IFIT2 (+1.99; 4.0e-20),
  IFI44 (+1.72; 3.3e-21), APOBEC3A (+1.66; 3.6e-14), APOBEC3B (+1.12; 0.017),
  plus IFN-regulatory/effector genes outside the provided signature:
  IRF7 (+1.32; 2.5e-22), STAT1 (+1.02; 6.2e-21), LY6E (+1.78), HERC5 (+1.70),
  RNF213 (+0.82), SAMD9 (+1.10), APOL6 (+0.83), TNFSF10/TRAIL (+1.18).
- Other up-regulated: MT2A (+1.58), PLAC8 (+1.18), TNFSF13B/BAFF (+0.60; FDR 3.5e-17),
  HSH2D (+0.88), PPM1K (+0.73), TYMP (+0.73).

DOWN-REGULATED IN SLE (log2FC; FDR)
- AP-1 immediate-early transcription factors: FOS (-0.36; 1.8e-05),
  JUND (-0.35; 4.3e-06) - core drivers of monocyte activation and cytokine production.
- Monocyte identity/housekeeping program (per-cell Wilcoxon concordant):
  LYZ, LST1, TYROBP, CTSS, CD74 (MHC-II invariant chain), FTH1/FTL, S100A4, S100A6, NAMPT.
- Additional edgeR down-genes: SORL1, HNRNPH1, TMEM107, SOX4, PTCH2, ARL4C, MAP4K5,
  ATP2B1, MS4A1, BLK, and lncRNAs (SNHG9, LINC00910).

EVIDENCE THAT THE UP-PROGRAM IS TYPE-I IFN DRIVEN
1. Of the provided 25-gene type-I ISG signature, 12 genes are measurable in this
   dataset (13, e.g. OAS1/2/3, MX1, SIGLEC1, RSAD2, EPSTI1, were author-filtered
   from the delivered gene universe). All 12 are up-regulated; mean log2FC +2.28
   vs +0.26 genome-wide background; CAMERA set-level test within the same model:
   Direction = Up, P = 2.8e-29.
2. Donor-level ISG score (mean log1p-CP10k of the 12 genes) separates every SLE
   group from controls: control 0.37 (n=99) < managed 0.97 (n=144) < flare 1.21
   (n=12) < treated 1.59 (n=6); Kruskal-Wallis p = 9.3e-21; SLE-vs-control
   Mann-Whitney AUC = 0.85.
3. Independent per-cell Wilcoxon cross-check (306,745 cells, donor-level
   normalization) agrees on direction: 148/280 edgeR-up genes also up per cell
   (45.6x enriched over chance); 189/191 edgeR-down genes also down; Spearman
   rho(edgeR logFC, Wilcoxon score) = 0.46. Per-cell top up-genes are the same
   ISGs (IFI6, IFITM3, IFI44L, ISG15, LY6E, IFI44, IFI27, IFIT3...).
4. The same IFN program appears in non-classical monocytes (252 FDR genes;
   top: ISG15, IFI27, IFI6, STAT1, IFI44L) and conventional DCs (112 FDR genes;
   top: IFI6, IFI44L, ISG15, IFITM3, IFI27), and a flare-vs-control contrast
   (n=12 flare donors) recapitulates it (IFI27 +4.37, CXCL10 +3.12, IFIT3 +2.33).
5. Robustness: dropping age/ethnicity/cohort from the model keeps 437/471 FDR
   genes; restricting to females (147 SLE / 97 controls) keeps 440/471; all 12
   signature genes remain up in both sensitivity runs.

INTERPRETATION
SLE classical monocytes are locked in a constitutive type-I interferon state:
up-regulation of the IFNAR -> JAK1/TYK2 -> STAT1/STAT2 -> IRF7 axis and its
antiviral/antiproliferative effectors (IFIT/IFI/ISG15/HERC5/APOBEC3A families),
plus the IFN-induced chemokine CXCL10 that can recruit CXCR3+ pDC and T cells and
sustain the loop. Simultaneously, AP-1 factors (FOS, JUND) and core monocyte
identity/antigen-presentation genes are down-regulated, consistent with IFN-driven
reprogramming of monocyte effector function. Therapeutically, the IFN pathway is
directly druggable and is the target of approved SLE biologics (anifrolumab,
anti-IFNAR1; refs: Furie NEJM 2019, Morand NEJM 2020), with CXCL10/CXCR3 and BAFF
(TNFSF13B) axes as additional druggable nodes.

CAVEATS
Genes were tested within the 1,889 author-retained gene universe (13/25 signature
genes unmeasurable); Processing_Cohort 1 contains only controls (cohort adjusted,
93% of findings robust to covariate choice); "treated" n=6 limits severity claims;
observational design - no causal ordering between IFN signaling, medication
exposure, and monocyte dysfunction.

FINAL ANSWER — Top signaling pathways predicted to mediate KIR+CD8+ T-cell suppression and cytotoxic targeting of CD4+ T cells in active celiac mucosa (beyond the MHC-I → CD3/CD8 baseline)

Cohort analyzed from the provided raw data: 10 mucosal biopsies (6 active CeD, 4 HC, GSE193442), 72,177 cells loaded; 56,586 cells x 15,835 genes after QC; Leiden clustering into 21 states. The KIR+ cytotoxic compartment was defined as cells with >=1 UMI across KIR2DL1/KIR2DL2DL3/KIR2DL4/KIR3DL1/KIR3DL2 within the 10 cytotoxic/gamma-delta clusters: 2,119 cells in CeD vs 585 in HC (3.6x expansion), strongly armed (GZMB 91%, PRF1 95%, GNLY 85%, FCGR3A +2.31 logFC vs KIR- cells, NKG2A/KLRC1 +2.41), with a CD8alpha-alpha / gamma-delta-IEL-like character (TRDC+ 38%, TRDV2+ 70%, CD8A+ 34%). CD4+ targets: 21,054 CeD vs 10,184 HC cells (2.1x expansion), activated (HLA-C +0.84, CD48, CXCR4, CCR7 up). Ligand-receptor inference used liana rank_aggregate (consensus of CellPhoneDB/NATMI/Connectome/SingleCellSignalR/logFC/geometric-mean; expr_prop 0.05, 1,000 permutations, seed 0), run separately per condition, direction KIR+CD8 -> CD4, with KIR- cytotoxic cells and the HC condition as controls, followed by a per-sample pseudobulk validation (n=6 CeD vs n=4 HC).

MHC-I (HLA-A/B/C -> CD3D/CD8A/CD8B) was recovered as the strongest baseline interaction (lr_means 0.81-0.86), as expected. The top pathways BEYOND MHC-I, ranked by combining significance in KIR+CD8-CeD -> CD4-CeD (56 of 89 pairs significant at permutation p <= 0.05), CeD specificity (46/56 pairs stronger in CeD), KIR+ specificity (49/56 pairs stronger from KIR+ than KIR- sources), and pseudobulk validation:

1. FASLG -> FAS / TNFRSF1A (death-receptor apoptosis) — the leading suppressive/cytotoxic candidate. FASLG in 10.0% of KIR+CD8-CeD vs 4.1% of KIR-CD8-CeD and 2.2% of KIR+CD8-HC; both FAS and TNFRSF1A pairs significant in CeD (permutation p = 0.0); per-donor ligand x receptor product is 6.9-fold higher in CeD than HC (0.0030 vs 0.0004; Welch p = 0.053, Mann-Whitney p = 0.067 at n=6 vs 4; every CeD-vs-HC comparison directional). Predicts Fas-mediated apoptosis of Fas+ CD4 targets as the main in-vitro killing route besides perforin/granzyme.

2. CCL5/CCL4 -> CXCR3 / CCR5 / DPP4 (effector chemokine axis) — strongest non-MHC-I magnitude among significant pairs (CCL5->DPP4 rank 0.364, CCL5->CXCR3 0.369, both p = 0.0) and the most KIR+-specific signals in the network (KIR+ specificity delta +0.080 and +0.081). CCL4 in 89% and CCL5 in 99% of KIR+CD8-CeD. Function: recruitment of chemokine-receptor+ CD4 cells into the effector-target contact zone rather than direct killing.

3. LGALS1 (galectin-1) -> CD45/PTPRC, CD69, ITGB1 (immunoregulatory lectin) — significant in CeD (p = 0.0), high in BOTH specificity contrasts (delta_CeD +0.028..+0.039; delta_KIR+ +0.048..+0.077), pseudobulk 2.0x in CeD (p = 0.059). The strongest candidate for active suppression of CD4 responses beyond cytotoxicity (galectin-1 induces T-cell apoptosis/tolerance).

4. MHC-II (HLA-DPB1/DQA1/DRB1/DQB1) -> CD4 — "MHC beyond MHC-I". KIR+ cells transcribe HLA-DPB1 (61%), HLA-DQA1 (49%), HLA-DRB1 (26%); HLA-DRB1->CD4 is the #2 CeD-specific pair overall (delta_CeD +0.043, delta_KIR+ +0.041; pseudobulk 2.15x). Direct killer-to-target contact; the proposed inhibitory MHC-II -> LAG3 route is only partially supported (LAG3 on 20% of KIR+ cells but receiver-side pairs not significant).

Tier 2: TGFB1 -> CXCR4/CD44 (TGFB1 in 50% of KIR+CD8-CeD; the only axis with pseudobulk p < 0.05, 1.39x, p = 0.046 — but weakest source attribution since Tregs also produce it); HMGB1 -> CXCR4 (delta_CeD +0.033, pseudobulk 1.34x, p = 0.062, alarmin-guided recruitment); TIMP1 -> CD63 (#1 CeD-specific pair, delta +0.055); FAM3C -> CLEC2D (LLT1) (novel inferred trans-inhibitory contact, delta +0.030).

Tier 3 (contact/co-stimulation): ITGB2 (LFA-1) -> CD226 (DNAM-1) (+0.041 KIR+-specific), SELPLG -> SELL/ITGB2, ADA/PAM -> DPP4. Explicit negatives: MIF -> CD44/CD74 and VIM -> CD44 are NOT KIR+- or CeD-specific (negative deltas) despite high magnitude; CD48 -> CD2 is generic T-T contact; HLA-E -> NKG2A-type autocrine circuitry not recoverable in target direction (permutation p = 1.0).

Overall interpretation: in active CeD the expanded KIR+ cytotoxic pool is wired for (i) contact-dependent killing of CD4 targets chiefly through FASLG-FAS (plus its granzyme/perforin program, expression-only evidence), (ii) chemokine-driven engagement of CXCR3/CCR5/DPP4+ CD4 cells, and (iii) suppression beyond killing through galectin-1, TGF-beta1, MHC-II-mediated contact and an LLT1/CLEC2D-type inhibitory axis.

Caveats: gliadin-specific CD4 cells cannot be identified from scRNA alone (targets = disease-enriched CD4 compartment); L-R inference is correlational and permutation treats cells as exchangeable (pseudobulk with n=6 vs 4 is conservative; FASLG axis p = 0.053); one CeD donor contributes 1,539/2,119 KIR+ cells; the KIR+ pool is CD8alpha-alpha/gamma-delta-like rather than pure alpha-beta CD8; myeloid/epithelial/stromal sources are absent (purified lymphocyte fraction), limiting cytokine axes (e.g., IFNG -> IFNGR: IFNG only 3% of KIR+ cells); KIR/HLA genotypes unavailable.

Evidence: all numbers from this run's outputs (trace.md section 4; tables under ccc-kir-cd8/output/tables/ including liana_focus_CeD.csv, pairwise_comparison_KIRplus.csv, axis_summary.csv, pseudobulk_group_stats.csv; methods in ccc-kir-cd8/README.md). Key external mechanisms: Strasser et al., Immunity 2009 (FAS); Rabinovich & Toscano, Nat Rev Immunol 2009 and Perillo et al., Nature 1995 (galectin-1); Li & Flavell, Cell 2008 (TGF-beta); Groom & Luster, Exp Cell Res 2011 (CXCR3); Meresse et al., Immunity 2004 / J Exp Med 2006 and Jabri & Sollid, Nat Rev Immunol 2009 (cytotoxic IEL biology in CeD); Efremova et al., NAR 2020 and Dimitrov et al., Nat Commun 2022 (inference methods).
grader_notes: The analysis is largely rigorous with careful QC, clustering, LR inference, and pathway ranking. However, omitted activated CD4 marker scoring, used a fixed rather than data-driven KIR threshold, did not identify gliadin-specific CD4 cells, and did not compute the reverse communication direction, preventing top marks in those criteria.

No. GAHT-induced protein changes are NOT consistent with those observed during menopause — they are predominantly ANTI-concordant with menopause and, instead, concordant with the protein signature of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) and of higher endogenous estradiol. In other words, 6 months of feminizing GAHT shifts the plasma proteome in a premenopausal, estrogen-replete direction.

Evidence (Olink Explore-HT, 2,791 proteins shared between Supplementary Tables 1 and 7; GAHT set = 258 proteins with adjusted p<0.05 in the CPA and/or SPIRO arm; 225 down / 33 up):

1) Versus menopause (<57): anti-concordant.
- Only 38/258 (14.7%) of GAHT-changed proteins move in the same direction as the menopause association (two-sided exact binomial p = 2.5e-32 vs 50% expected).
- Mean menopause coefficient within the GAHT set is +0.0700 (one-sample Wilcoxon p = 3.0e-25): proteins that menopause RAISES are proteins GAHT LOWERS.
- 86.0% (222/258) of the GAHT set is significantly menopause-associated (enrichment vs 5% background, p = 3.2e-246), and among proteins significant in both analyses, 89.4% (160/179, CPA arm) and 83.6% (61/73, SPIRO arm) show OPPOSITE signs.
- Full-proteome Spearman rho(GAHT z-score, menopause estimate) = -0.186 (2,000-permutation p = 5.0e-4).
- Direction split: the anti-menopausal signal is driven by the 225 GAHT-down proteins, which are elevated in the menopause comparison (+0.0791, p = 3.6e-25).

2) Versus MHT: concordant.
- Sign concordance 72.1% (186/258) with MHT<57 (binomial p = 8.4e-13) and 80.2% (207/258) with MHT>=57 (p = 1.8e-23).
- 54.7% (141/258) and 45.3% (117/258) of the GAHT set is MHT-significant — a ~9.2-9.5-fold enrichment over the 5% background (p <= 7.0e-111).
- Among proteins significant in both GAHT (per arm) and MHT, 77-95% share the same sign (e.g., 84/109 CPA-MHT<57; 41/43 SPIRO-MHT>=57; Fisher p <= 9.1e-7). Full-proteome rho with MHT>=57 = +0.111 (perm p = 5.0e-4).

3) Versus endogenous estradiol in women (ln-E2): concordant — the strongest positive full-proteome correlation measured (Spearman rho = +0.169, perm p = 5.0e-4; 72.1% sign concordance in the GAHT set, p = 8.4e-13).

4) Versus testosterone: anti-concordant as mechanistically expected for an antiandrogen+estradiol regimen (sign concordance 31.0% with ln-testosterone in women, p = 9.8e-10; 38.0% in men, p = 1.4e-4). GAHT suppresses androgen-driven proteins (e.g., SPINT3 -7.90, INSL3 -5.35, EDDM3B -2.64, TEX101 -2.09 in CPA), while estrogen-responsive hepatic proteins move as under MHT (SHBG +0.28/+0.29 vs MHT +0.085 and ln-E2 +0.170; fibrinogen FGA and prekallikrein KLKB1 trend down on GAHT but rise with menopause).

5) Robustness: results are consistent across the CPA and SPIRO regimens (menopause concordance 21.7% vs 17.5%; MHT<57 66.5% vs 82.5%; MHT>=57 74.1% vs 80.0%), across correlation metrics, and in composite signatures (estrogenic signature rho = +0.122, perm p = 5.0e-4; androgenic signature within the GAHT set rho = -0.254).

Interpretation: exogenous estradiol plus androgen suppression reproduces the estrogen-REPLENT (premenopausal) protein state, whereas natural menopause reflects estrogen LOSS — the two interventions move the same proteins in opposite directions, and MHT (estrogen re-addition after menopause) moves them the same way GAHT does. Exceptions exist at the individual-protein level (e.g., leptin rises on GAHT and is also higher in menopause comparisons; CPA-specific prolactin rise).

STATISTICAL TEST USED
Primary test: two-sided Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum) comparing TotalNonSyn (total somatic non-synonymous SNVs per patient) between responders and non-responders. Chosen because TML is strongly right-skewed (group max 3,985 vs median 489) with unequal variances (R SD 918.7 vs NR SD 489.6), violating t-test assumptions. Supporting tests: univariate and covariate-adjusted logistic regression (likelihood-ratio p), Spearman rank correlation, point-biserial correlation, and Fisher's exact test on a median split.

KEY NUMBERS
- Median TML: responders 495 nsSNVs [IQR 313-807] vs non-responders 281 nsSNVs [IQR 232-621]; responders/non-responders median ratio = 1.76x. Means: 817.9 vs 536.8.
- Mann-Whitney U = 214, p = 0.304 (two-sided): NOT significant at alpha = 0.05.
- Association metrics: Cliff's delta (rank-biserial) = 0.199; Goodman-Kruskal gamma = 0.199; dominance odds ratio = 1.50; ROC AUC = 0.599 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.406-0.784, includes 0.5).
- Correlations: Spearman rho = 0.171 (p = 0.304); point-biserial r = 0.186 (p = 0.264).
- Logistic regression: OR per 100 additional nsSNVs = 1.062 (95% CI 0.952-1.185), p(LLR) = 0.227; per 1 SD of TML, OR = 1.584. Adjusting for tumor purity, ploidy and WES coverage, TML OR = 1.090 (0.946-1.255), p = 0.233.
- Secondary burden measures show the same positive direction, all non-significant: expressed nsSNVs (median 335 vs 250, p = 0.628), non-synonymous indels (3 vs 2, p = 0.171), HLA-I neoepitope binders (231 vs 156, p = 0.411), strong binders (117 vs 88, p = 0.318). Smallest p in the 5-test family (0.171) does not survive Bonferroni (alpha = 0.01).
- Sensitivity analyses (all remain non-significant, same direction): excluding the 7 BRCA2-mutant tumors, U = 138, p = 0.489; excluding the two highest-TML patients (Pt4 3,985 and Pt27 2,297, both responders), U = 180, p = 0.568; median split at 489 nsSNVs gives Fisher exact OR = 1.24, p = 1.0 (10/19 low-TML vs 11/19 high-TML responders).
- Best exploratory TML cutoff (in-sample Youden): >= 312 nsSNVs gives sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.53.

INTERPRETATION
The direction of the association matches the neoantigen model of checkpoint-blockade response (more mutated peptides -> more HLA-presented neoantigens -> more T cells reactivated by PD-1 blockade; Snyder 2014, Rizvi 2015, Schumacher & Schreiber 2015), and the responder median is 1.76x the non-responder median. However, at n = 38 the single-metric TML signal is weak (AUC approx. 0.6) and does not reach statistical significance; the 95% CI for AUC includes 0.5. Response to anti-PD-1 in melanoma is also driven by TML-independent mechanisms (e.g., IPRES transcriptional resistance program, antigen-presentation/JAK-pathway defects), which dilute the TML-response association.

LIMITATIONS
Underpowered at n = 38 for moderate effects (~80% power only for AUC >= ~0.78); cannot claim "no association" either - the CI spans both no effect and a moderate effect. Binary irRECIST labels do not capture depth/durability of benefit. Confounder adjustment is limited to purity, ploidy and coverage (no stage/MAPKi-history/microbiome modeling). TML here counts non-synonymous SNVs only and is not normalized per megabase as in modern panel-TMB conventions.
